My wife and I watch a lot of the same shows, and we're bad at keeping up with them. We miss that a
new season started, or that a finale aired last week, and every so often we'd like a suggestion that isn't
just "more of the same." I wanted something that would check every morning and hand us a short
stack of cards: *new episode*, *season date announced*, *you might like this*, *news about a show you
watch*. We tap **Noted** and the card goes away.

The app is private: it only works for our two Google accounts. So this post is screenshots
and a write-up of how it's built, and of what went wrong along the way.

<!-- TODO(screenshot): Feed view on a phone, 3-4 cards visible -->

## The first plan, and why it changed

The original idea was simple: have ChatGPT do a daily web search about our shows and write what it
found into a spreadsheet. Then an app reads the spreadsheet.

The problem showed up as soon as I wrote down the cards I wanted. *"New episode of {show} released on
{date}, {title}, {IMDb link}"* is all specifics. Titles, air dates, air times, links and poster
images are exactly what a web-searching LLM gets slightly wrong, and a wrong air date is worse than no
air date. Structured TV databases, though, have all of it for free:

- **TMDB** has episodes, season air dates, posters, IMDb IDs and a "next episode to air".
- **TVmaze** has the actual broadcast schedule, with air times, including streaming drop dates.

So the design became a hybrid. **APIs for facts, the LLM for taste.** The LLM does two jobs a
database can't:

- **Suggestions:** shows we might like, given what we track and what we've rejected.
- **News:** renewals, cancellations, trailers and casting news, often before the databases catch up.

## How it fits together

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[GitHub Actions<br/>6 am daily] --> J[Python job]
  J -->|facts| T[(TMDB / TVmaze)]
  J -->|suggestions + news| O[OpenAI<br/>web search]
  J -->|append cards,<br/>rewrite schedule| S[(Google Sheet)]
  P[Web app<br/>on GitHub Pages] <-->|read cards,<br/>write Noted / Track| S
```

There are two programs, and they never talk to each other. The Sheet is the whole interface between
them:

- **The job**, a Python script on a GitHub Actions cron, adds rows and rewrites the schedule.
- **The app**, a static page, reads the Sheet and flips a `status` cell when you tap a button.

## A spreadsheet as a database

Using a Google Sheet as the only datastore is either a great idea or a terrible one, depending on how
disciplined you are about it. It's great because you can open it and *see* the state, fix a typo by
hand, and there's no server to run. It's terrible because it has no transactions, no locks, and nothing
stops two writers from stepping on each other.

What made it work was a few rules:

- **Rows are never deleted or reordered.** Untracking a show sets `active = FALSE` instead of
  deleting the row, so a row number read a minute ago still points at the same row.
- **Every column has exactly one writer.** The job writes card content (titles, dates, images). The
  app writes `status`. Early on I had the job moving season cards to a `superseded` status. A design
  review pointed out that if you tapped Noted between the job's read and its write, the job would
  overwrite your tap. The fix was a separate job-owned `current` column. The feed shows a card
  only when `status = new` *and* `current = TRUE`, so neither writer ever touches the other's cell.
- **Card IDs are deterministic**, e.g. `ep:{show}:S02E05` or `season:{show}:3:2026-12-01`, and the job
  never appends an ID that already exists. Running the job twice in one day is a no-op. The first
  GitHub Actions run, right after a local one, appended zero cards, which is exactly what you want.

Putting the date in the season card's ID turned out nicely. If a premiere date moves, that's a new ID,
so a new card, and the old card goes `current = FALSE`. If the date moves *back*, the original card
becomes current again.

## The LLM proposes, the code confirms

Nothing the LLM says reaches the Sheet without being checked by ordinary code.

**Suggestions are confirmed against TMDB.** The model returns just a title, a year and a one-line
reason. The job searches TMDB for that title and year, and only a real match becomes a card. The ID,
poster and link all come from TMDB, never from the model. A made-up show simply fails the lookup and
disappears.

**News can't be confirmed the same way**, since there's no database of TV news to check against. So it
gets a weaker, explicit trust level: *cited, not confirmed*:

1. The article URL must be one the web search tool **actually returned**. The OpenAI Responses API
   will list the sources it retrieved if you ask (`include: ["web_search_call.action.sources"]`).
2. The job fetches the page and reads its own publish date from the metadata. If that date falls
   outside the last 7 days, the item is dropped.
3. The card always shows the source's domain, so we can judge it ourselves.

```python
elif key not in allowed:
    dropped.append(f"{headline}: URL not among search sources")
elif (html := fetch(url)) is None:
    dropped.append(f"{headline}: page unreachable")
elif not cutoff <= published <= today:
    dropped.append(f"{headline}: published {published}, outside window")
```

## Debugging an empty news feed

Before building any of the Sheet or app plumbing, I wrote a `--dry-run` that runs the two LLM calls
against a hand-written list of shows and prints everything, including what got dropped and why.
Suggestions were good from the first run. News came back **empty**, every time.

The instinct is to start rewording the prompt. It's more useful to find out *why* first. I asked the
API for the model's reasoning summaries (`reasoning: {"summary": "auto"}`), printed every search query
it ran, and found four separate problems, each needing a different fix:

1. **My sample list was actually quiet.** One show had ended, one had been renewed a year earlier, and one
   was between seasons. For those three, "no news this week" was the right answer. I'd assumed a month
   must have *something*, and it didn't.
2. **The prompt told the model to self-filter.** It said "an empty list is a good answer", and asked for
   news "published in the last 7 days". So when the model found relevant articles but couldn't confirm
   their exact dates from the search snippets, it played safe and returned nothing. But the code already
   checks the date from the page itself. The fix was to tell the model to *propose* everything that might
   qualify, with its best-guess date, and let the code decide.
3. **It made up the source URL.** It read a story on one site, then cited a Variety URL it had never
   retrieved, presumably because the prompt asked for "the original report where possible". The source
   check dropped it, which was correct. The prompt now says to use only URLs from the search results.
4. **It embedded citations in the JSON.** Suggestion reasons arrived with inline markdown links like
   `([themoviedb.org](…?utm_source=openai))`. Those are now stripped in code, *and* the prompt asks for
   plain text. The code is what guarantees it; the prompt just reduces how often the code has to.

Two more observations. Identical runs gave 0 items and then 1, so a single dry run tells you very
little. And reasoning effort mattered for news, though not for suggestions:

| News call | Input tokens | Searches | Found the test story |
|---|---|---|---|
| effort `low` | ~30k | 4 | no |
| effort `medium` | ~80k | 9 | yes |

News now runs at `medium` and suggestions at `low`. Nearly all of those tokens are the search results
the tool pulls in, not my prompt.

## Auth without a backend

The app is a static page on GitHub Pages, with no server of mine behind it. It signs in with Google
(the token flow from Google Identity Services) and calls the Sheets API directly from the browser,
using your own token.

That means **the Sheet's sharing settings are the access control.** The Sheet is shared with exactly
three accounts: mine, my wife's, and the job's service account. Anyone can load the page and even sign
in, but the first read returns a 403 and they see "This app is private". There's nothing to protect
in the page itself, because the data isn't in the page.

Two surprises here:

- **Google's "Testing" mode expires consent every 7 days.** I'd planned to use its test-user list as a
  free allowlist, but a weekly re-consent screen is the kind of friction that makes you stop using a
  thing. Publishing the OAuth app to Production *without* verification avoids that. The costs are a
  one-time "Google hasn't verified this app" screen, and filling in a home page, a privacy policy and an
  authorized domain before Google lets you publish.
- **A wrong-account sign-in was a dead end.** The final code review spotted it. The app saved the token
  so you wouldn't have to sign in on every visit, but if you'd signed in with an account that didn't
  have the Sheet, every reload reused that token, got a 403, and showed "private" for an hour. Now a
  403 clears the saved token and offers "Use another account".

## What the reviews caught

I had a fresh reviewer read each piece before it shipped. Almost everything they caught was a
mismatch between my code and the real world, exactly where the fake spreadsheet in my tests couldn't
help:

- **The Sheet's locale.** Reading cells "as displayed" returns booleans in the spreadsheet's language.
  A Sheet created from a French-Canadian account shows `VRAI`/`FAUX`, so every show would have looked
  inactive. The job would have processed nothing, reported success, and exited cleanly. Both the job
  and the app now read unformatted values.
- **Public logs.** A GitHub Pages repo is public, so its Actions logs are too. My job printed the
  names of any shows that failed to refresh. It now logs "show 3 of 11" and keeps the names in the
  Sheet's private status tab.
- **A schedule special that TVmaze didn't list.** A Halloween special was in TMDB but missing from TVmaze,
  and the schedule was built from TVmaze alone. This one came from real output rather than a review,
  but it was the same kind of gap. The schedule now falls back to TMDB's next episode.

## Cost

Per day, about 20k input tokens and 2 searches for suggestions, plus about 70–80k input tokens and 8–9
searches for news. Everything else is free: TMDB, TVmaze, GitHub Actions and Pages, and the Sheets API.

## What's next

A week of real cards will show whether news dedupe holds up over time, and whether suggestions get
repetitive once a few have been ignored. For the next post, the interesting question is whether the
"ignored" list actually steers the model away from *similar* shows, or only stops the exact ones we
rejected.
